1: vicinae is a multi purpose launcher built with QtQuick. This file focuses on explaining general rules. For everything else, just look at the codebase.
2: 
3: It uses QML for presentation and C++ for business logic.
4: React/Typescript is used to power the extension API.
5: 
6: For development: 
7: - On UNIXes, use `make dev`.
8: - On Windows use `cmake --preset windows-relwithdebinfo` (full debug builds only when needed)
9: 
10: ## Separation of concerns
11: 
12: QML is exclusively used for presentation. DO NOT put business logic inside QML files.
13: It's okay to make small JavaScript functions and utilities as long as their purpose is to help deal with presentation concerns.
14: 
15: To implement views, we use a bridge pattern: a C++ "view host" class exposes data and actions as `Q_PROPERTY`s and `Q_INVOKABLE`s, and a QML component binds to them.
16: 
17: Remain pragmatic about this, we don't want to go back and forth between QML and C++ to execute 2 lines of logic. But most of the time, the separation is clear.
18: 
19: ## C++/QT coding rules
20: 
21: We use C++23 so we have access to most modern C++ features. 
22: Here are a few rules to keep in mind:
23: 
24: - Lack of value: use `std::optional` instead of arbitrary value discriminants such as the empty string. If this is not possible or goes against a commonly used convention, respect the convention first, no shoehorning. If we are dealing with raw pointers, the nullable component is already part of it so no need to add a layer of indirection.
25: - Prefer `std::array` to C arrays where it makes sense. You can use `std::to_array` to initialize them automatically sized from an initializer list.
26: - C symbols: always use the `std::` prefix for symbols coming from C headers (`std::uint64_t`, `std::size_t`, `std::memset`, `std::getenv`, ...) and include the `<c*>` header form. POSIX-only symbols (`ssize_t`, `recv`, ...) have no `std::` counterpart and stay unprefixed.
27: - use `constexpr` and `consteval` as much as possible, we want to move what we can at compile time.
28: - Avoid raw pointers: unless we are dealing with QT's ownership model or a C API. For QT classes that are not QObjects, you should probably use standard smart pointers as recommended in modern QT. 
29: - QObjects must be deleted using `deleteLater` and never raw `delete`, as this can cause memory corruption with signal and slots. Calling `delete` on a `QObject` is a **STRONG** code smell.
30: - Watch for implicit copies: avoid copies as much as possible, use non owning containers when you can (`std::span`, `std::string_view`, `QStringView`) and just `std::move` the data when applicable. When copy is the safest option, use copy: don't go out of your way to respect this rule.
31: - QT vs STL classes: prefer STL containers over QT counterparts.
32: - vectors: always reserve `std::vector`s and use `emplace_back` to push new elements.
33: - STL ranges: we like to use `<ranges>` where it works well. If you need to use a `for` loop, prioritize ranged ones or use `std::views::enumerate` if you need to deal with indexes and data.
34: - casts: as you may notice from the clang-tidy rules, using `static_cast` is generally discouraged for classes that are related by inheritance, as it is very easy to make mistakes. Unless the logic is in a hot path (e.g a QT event filter), it's preferrable to use `dynamic_cast` as a safety net when there is no safer option. Note however that `dynamic_cast` is STILL a code smell and should generally be avoided in favor of better polymorphism.
35: - Platform guards: use Qt's `Q_OS_*` macros (`Q_OS_MACOS`, `Q_OS_LINUX`, `Q_OS_WIN`) rather than `Q_OS_DARWIN` or compiler-defined ones like `__APPLE__`. `Q_OS_MACOS` specifically targets desktop macOS (excluding iOS/tvOS) and keeps guards consistent across the codebase.
36: - As Vicinae becomes cross-platform, it is really important that we implement functionality the way it is intended to on the target platform. We should avoid using weird hacks and always use native APIs when possible.
37: 
38: ## Coding style
39: 
40: - For QObject classes: always put `Q_OBJECT`, `Q_PROPERTY`, `Q_INVOKABLE`, and `signals` on top of the class, in this order.
41: - Do not add unnecessary comments. Use them sparingly when something really needs to be made explicit.
42: - Include order: system headers before local headers.
43: - Header guards: use `#pragma once`.
44: - String types: use `std::string` internally, `QString` only at the Qt boundary.
45: - Constants: use `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE` for `constexpr` and `static const` values.
46: - Do not overuse comments, only add them when they provide actual value
47: 
48: ## Linting and formatting
49: 
50: We format all our code using `clang-format`. We have a `make format` rule that will automatically format the entire codebase if necessary.
51: 
52: To format the codebase:
53: 
54: - On UNIXes, run `make format`
55: - On Windows, run the PowerShell script at `.\scripts\format.ps1`
56: 
57: ALWAYS run `make format` at the end of a development session to make sure formatting is properly applied to all files.
58: 
59: All our code is also linted with `clang-tidy` in order to make detecting common mistakes easier. `clang-tidy` violations may be acceptable under some circumstances, and should be implemented using `//NOLINTBEGIN(<rule>)` and `NOLINTEND(<rule>)`. comments. Inline `//NOLINT` comments are generally discouraged because they can break after formatting. If a nolint directive does not work (e.g we're dealing with an internal STL false positive) then you can do a local override of the `clang-tidy` configuration to explicitly disable the faulty check.
60: 
61: ## QML rules
62: 
63: QML code should pass the linter, which you can run using `make qmllint`.
64: 
65: When writing JavaScript inside QML files, use ES6 syntax to the largest extent possible.
66: 
67: Try to keep the amount of logic in these files small. Logic in QML is only for presentation concerns: metrics computation, hover on signal, etc...
68: 
69: Some configuration and theming options may need to be accessed directly in QML. We expose a global config and theme bridges for this use case.
70: 
71: ## Code generation
72: 
73: There are two main families of code generation in the codebase:
74: 
75: - IPC, used by the CLI, the input server, and the extension runtime. This uses our own generator `figura` which is directly compiled in tree and invoked when needed.
76: - Generating of static datasets, such as emoji/symbol lists. We generally generate these using some typescript or python scripts, but do not make them part of the build system. We regenerate the lists from time to time, depending on the usecase. For example we have a `make genicon` and `make emoji` rules.
77: 
78: ## Internationalization
79: 
80: User-visible natural-language strings must be marked for translation. English source text is the translation key.
81: 
82: - QML: wrap literals in `qsTr("...")`.
83: - C++ classes with `Q_OBJECT`: use `tr("...")`.
84: - C++ classes without `Q_OBJECT`: NEVER call the inherited `tr()` (it resolves to the wrong context at runtime). Add `Q_DECLARE_TR_FUNCTIONS(ClassName)` at the top of the class, or for a single string use `QCoreApplication::translate("ClassName", "...")`.
85: - Never store translated strings in `static`/`constexpr` data. Plurals use `tr("%n item(s)", nullptr, n)`. Never concatenate translated fragments: use `%1` placeholders with `.arg()`.
86: - Preserve brand and product names such as "Raycast Store", "Raycast Compat", and "Extension Store". Translate the surrounding prose, not the name itself.
87: - Never translate stable technical notation such as ids, acronyms, unit symbols (`MB`, `GB`), filenames, protocol names, icon names (`ImageURL::builtin`), log output, storage keys, or strings compared as discriminants.
88: - Use natural, concise language appropriate for a desktop launcher. Prefer familiar UI wording over literal translations, bureaucratic language, or an excessively formal or polite tone.
89: - Use the platform's official localized terminology for operating-system features and settings pages.
90: - Use stable explicit translation contexts for shared domain strings. Add translator notes or disambiguation only when the source text is genuinely ambiguous.
91: - Source text and location metadata in `src/server/translations/*.ts` are generated: never hand-edit them. Edit
92:   translations with Qt Linguist. Contributors are not required to translate new strings or include regenerated catalogs in
93:   feature PRs. Maintainers periodically run `make update-translations` in dedicated localization updates.
94: 
95: ## General guidelines
96: 
97: - Search should always be fuzzy, unless it has a good reason not to. We have fuzzy utilities already, and we like to use our fuzzy trait system by specializing the `FuzzySearchable` template
98: - We are building Vicinae with cross-platform compatibility in mind (Linux, MacOS, Windows) so abstractions need to be designed accordingly. While Linux is our main development target, we should avoid making abstractions that are too platform specific.
99: 
100: ## React/TypeScript extensions
101: 
102: Everything related to the Typescript SDK can be found under `src/typescript`. More information can be obtained by reading `README.md` files under this directory if you need to work on this part. 
103:

# Role & Mission
You are a Principal Systems Engineer and Software Architect specializing in C++23, Qt6/QML, and modern Linux desktop environments (Wayland/X11). 
Your task is to analyze the extracted internals of Raycast (from the bundled DMG) to identify candidate core built-in features, rigorously filter them against a bloat/feasibility rubric, and incrementally port only high-value, native logic into Vicinae without introducing instability, bloat, or architectural drift.

You can use /rea  /ponytail when needed

---

### Context & Architectural Baseline
1. **Source Target (Raycast)**:
   - Extracted JavaScript backend services (`macos-app_RaycastDesktopApp.bundle/Contents/Resources/backend/index.mjs`).
   - Native modules (`calculator-rs`, `data`, `indexer`, `process-utils`).
   - Known built-in systems: Calculator/unit conversion, Clipboard history, Snippet expansion, Quicklinks, Window management layouts, Notes, Color formatting, Browser extension sync (`bext`).

2. **Destination Target (Vicinae)**:
   - Core Architecture: Modern C++23 for business logic and services (`vicinae/src/server/src/`); QtQuick / QML for presentation (`vicinae/src/server/src/ui/`).
   - Extension & Bridge Runtime: Node.js/TypeScript extension runtime with `raycast-api-compat` and `figura` IPC generator.
   - Design Constraints: Governed strictly by `vicinae/AGENTS.md` (bridge pattern with `Q_PROPERTY`/`Q_INVOKABLE`, strict separation between QML and C++, modern STL over Qt containers, `deleteLater` for QObjects, `FuzzySearchable` traits for search).

---

### Phase 1: Feature Evaluation & Anti-Bloat Rubric (Decision Gate)
Before writing or proposing any code, evaluate any potential Raycast built-in against this mandatory 4-point gate. If a feature fails even one gate, REJECT or DEFER it.

1. **The Extension vs. Core Test**:
   - *Question*: Can this feature be shipped as a TypeScript/React extension instead of native C++?
   - *Rule*: If it does not require sub-millisecond hotkeys, background system hooks, or tight Qt window integration, it MUST NOT be added to the C++ core. Keep the C++ binary lean.

2. **The Platform Agnosticism Test**:

# Core Built-in Gap Analysis: Raycast DMG vs. Vicinae

---

## 1. Architectural Baseline Comparison

| System | Raycast (`Raycast_2.10.1.0_arm64.dmg`) | Vicinae (`./vicinae`) | Key Difference |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Shell & UI** | macOS AppKit + Swift Mach-O host (`Contents/MacOS/Raycast`) | C++23 + Qt6/QtQuick QML (`vicinae/src/server/src/ui/`) | Raycast is macOS AppKit-native; Vicinae is cross-platform Wayland/X11/macOS native. |
| **Backend Core** | Bundled Node.js (`backend/index.mjs`, ~8.1 MB) + native Mach-O `.node` addons | High-performance C++23 services (`vicinae/src/server/src/services/`) | Raycast runs heavy JS in the background; Vicinae runs sub-millisecond compiled C++. |
| **Extension SDK** | `@raycast/api` (React Reconciler communicating with host) | [`vicinae/src/typescript/raycast-api-compat`](file:///home/prem/Projects/Raycat/vicinae/src/typescript/raycast-api-compat) + [`@vicinae/api`](file:///home/prem/Projects/Raycat/vicinae/src/typescript/api) | Vicinae runs extensions via Node/TS worker bridged via `figura` IPC into the C++ core. |
| **Quicklinks** | Rich template engine (`backend/index.mjs` ~L1.98M): URL encoding, modifiers (`| uppercase`, `| trim`, `| percent-encode`), fallbacks (`??`), and date offsets | [`Shortcut`](file:///home/prem/Projects/Raycat/vicinae/src/server/src/services/shortcut/shortcut.hpp) & [`expandShortcut`](file:///home/prem/Projects/Raycat/vicinae/src/server/src/actions/shortcut-actions.hpp#L27-L53) | Vicinae has placeholder parsing (`{clipboard}`, `{selected}`, `{uuid}`, `{argument}`), but lacks percent-encoding, modifiers, fallbacks, and date offsets. |
| **Snippets** | Dynamic placeholders (`{cursor}`, `{clipboard}`, `{date offset="+1d"}`, `{time}`, `{selection}`, modifiers) | [`SnippetExpander`](file:///home/prem/Projects/Raycat/vicinae/src/server/src/services/snippet/snippet-expander.hpp) + Linux `uinput` daemon (`vicinae/src/snippet/`) | Vicinae already has a daemon, cursor tracking, and shell execution, but lacks date arithmetic offsets, time units, and string modifiers. |
| **Calculator** | Custom parser (`calculator-rs`) + `Calculator.node` (SoulverCore wrapper on macOS) | Abstract backend architecture: `qalculate` (`libqalculate`), `soulver-core`, `numen` | Vicinae's `libqalculate` backend on Linux is computationally superior, but its root search intent detection hides results if fuzzy matches exist. |
| **Fuzzy Search** | Custom keyword & recency weighting | `fzf` algorithm ([`fzf.hpp`](file:///home/prem/Projects/Raycat/vicinae/src/lib/fuzzy/include/fuzzy/fzf.hpp)) + frecency decay ([`root-item-manager.cpp`](file:///home/prem/Projects/Raycat/vicinae/src/server/src/services/root-item-manager/root-item-manager.cpp#L144-L160)) | Vicinae already uses `fzf` with weighted strings (title: 1.0, unlocalized: 1.0, subtitle: 0.5, alias: 1.0, keywords: 0.6). |

---

## 2. Decision Gate Scoring Matrix

Each candidate is evaluated against our 4 mandatory gates:
1. **Extension vs. Core Test**: Must require sub-ms latency, desktop hooks, or tight Qt window integration; otherwise reject or move to TS.
2. **Platform Agnosticism Test**: Must not rely on proprietary macOS private APIs (AppKit, Carbon, AppleScript); must use standard Linux/Qt abstractions.
3. **Performance & Memory Budget**: No background polling, zero disk bottlenecks, <16ms frame deadline on launch path.
4. **Maintenance & Clean-Room**: Zero copied code; cleanly reimplement specifications and algorithms in C++23.

| Feature Candidate | Gate 1: Core Required? | Gate 2: Platform Agnostic? | Gate 3: Budget (<16ms)? | Gate 4: Clean-Room Spec? | Verdict |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **1. Quicklink Dynamic Templates & Percent-Encoding** | **PASS** (Core fallback & action panel) | **PASS** (Pure string & `QUrl`) | **PASS** (<0.5ms sync) | **PASS** (Format spec) | **APPROVED (High ROI)** |
| **2. Snippet Expansion Math & Modifiers** | **PASS** (Core `uinput` expander) | **PASS** (`QDateTime` + STL) | **PASS** (<0.2ms sync) | **PASS** (Offset grammar) | **APPROVED (High ROI)** |
| **3. Calculator Intent Detection in Root Search** | **PASS** (Core search model) | **PASS** (Regex / tokenizer) | **PASS** (Non-blocking / lazy) | **PASS** (Grammar heuristic) | **APPROVED (High ROI)** |
| **4. AI Chat Window & MCP Hub** | **FAIL** (Better as TS/React extension) | **PASS** (HTTP/SSE) | **WARN** (Heavy memory/state) | **PASS** | **DEFER to Extension** |
| **5. Window Snapping / Positioning Presets** | **PASS** (Core WM) | **FAIL** (Wayland compositor fragmentation) | **PASS** | **PASS** | **REJECT** |
| **6. Cloud Sync Agent (`sync_agent.db`)** | **FAIL** (Daemon/Plugin) | **PASS** | **FAIL** (Background I/O & lock contention) | **FAIL** (Proprietary backend) | **REJECT (Bloat)** |

---

## 3. Top 3 Recommended Enhancements

### Enhancement 1: Quicklinks / Shortcuts Dynamic Template Engine & Percent-Encoding
- **Why it matters**: Currently, in [`expandShortcut`](file:///home/prem/Projects/Raycat/vicinae/src/server/src/actions/shortcut-actions.hpp#L27-L53), arguments are directly concatenated into the URL string without percent-encoding:
  ```cpp
  // Current behavior in vicinae:
  expanded += args[argumentIndex++]; // If user inputs "apple pie", URL becomes "...?q=apple pie" (invalid)
  ```
  This breaks web searches and API links with spaces or symbols. Furthermore, default values specified in `{argument name="q" default="vicinae"}` are ignored during expansion.
- **What we extract from Raycast**:
  - Auto URL/percent-encoding for query components (`QUrl::toPercentEncoding`).
  - Argument fallback values when input is empty.
  - Modifiers: `| percent-encode`, `| trim`, `| uppercase`, `| lowercase`.
  - Fallback placeholder chain: `{selection ?? clipboard ?? argument name="query"}`.
- **Architectural Fit**: Pure C++23 changes within [`Shortcut`](file:///home/prem/Projects/Raycat/vicinae/src/server/src/services/shortcut/shortcut.hpp) and [`shortcut-actions.hpp`](file:///home/prem/Projects/Raycat/vicinae/src/server/src/actions/shortcut-actions.hpp). No new dependencies, zero latency impact.

### Enhancement 2: Snippet Date Arithmetic & String Modifiers
- **Why it matters**: Vicinae's [`SnippetExpander`](file:///home/prem/Projects/Raycat/vicinae/src/server/src/services/snippet/snippet-expander.hpp#L60-L100) already supports `{cursor}`, `{clipboard}`, `{uuid}`, and static `{date format="..."}`. However, power users regularly rely on date offsets (e.g., `{date offset="+1d" format="yyyy-MM-dd"}` or `{date -1w}`) and formatted time units (`{time}`, `{day}`).
- **What we extract from Raycast**:
  - The offset grammar discovered in Raycast's `Rmn()` / `Lmn()`: `[+-][0-9]+[dwmyh]` (Days, Weeks, Months, Years, Hours).
  - Clean C++ evaluation using `QDateTime::addDays()`, `addMonths()`, `addYears()`, `addSecs()`.
  - Modifier pipeline: `{clipboard | uppercase}`, `{clipboard | trim}`.
- **Architectural Fit**: Contained completely inside [`SnippetExpander`](file:///home/prem/Projects/Raycat/vicinae/src/server/src/services/snippet/snippet-expander.hpp). Executed on-demand when expanding snippet triggers, adding <0.1ms overhead.

### Enhancement 3: Calculator Intent Heuristic in Root Search
- **Why it matters**: In Vicinae's [`RootSearchModel::refreshCalculator`](file:///home/prem/Projects/Raycat/vicinae/src/server/src/builtins/root/root-search-model.cpp#L173-L190):
  ```cpp
  if (m_resultsSource->count() > 0 || m_query.size() < CALCULATOR_MIN_CHARS) return;
  ```
  If typing `24 * 7` or `50 usd in eur` matches any file, command, or app title loosely, the calculator card is completely hidden unless the user explicitly prefixes with `=`. 
- **What we extract from Raycast**:
  - A fast, non-allocating math intent heuristic (checks if query starts with numbers followed by math operators `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `^`, or unit keywords `in`, `to`).
  - When math intent is detected, compute via the existing `m_calculator->backend()` and present the calculator card above lower-quality fuzzy matches.
- **Architectural Fit**: Plugs directly into `RootSearchModel` without touching QML presentation layers or calculator backends.

---

### What We Skip & Remaining Risks
- **Skipped**: Window management positioning (Wayland protocol fragmentation across GNOME/KDE/wlroots makes external window snapping fragile) and Cloud sync (proprietary network bloat).
- **Risk**: Any changes to snippet expansion run right before uinput keyboard event injection; unit tests must verify edge-case formatting so invalid syntax does not cause unexpected backspaces.

Window snapping and tiling's implementation varies, depending on the OS: Raycast uses Accessibility APIs on macOS, while Linux relies on the Wayland compositor or X11 WM. The challenge involves unifying resizing functionality across diverse windowing environments.


The Linux implementation relying on platform-specific hacks fails the Platform Agnosticism Test; a launcher should not depend on brittle, unstandardized Wayland interactions. Checking the four decision gates to evaluate candidates.

Candidate 1, Dynamic Template Placeholders & URL Encoding for Quicklinks/Shortcuts, appears to be a good candidate because it's unlikely to require the C++ core or introduce significant performance bottlenecks. It does not appear to need deep platform integration, so it should pass the Platform Agnosticism Test and Maintenance & Clean-Room Test if implemented correctly.


Dynamic Template Placeholders & URL Encoding for Quicklinks/Shortcuts appears to pass all decision gates. The implementation handles percent-encoding for URL queries, supports modifiers for arguments (trim, uppercase, percent-encode), default values for arguments, and date/time manipulation with offsets and formatting. The extension's logic cleanly reimplements standard template replacement in C++23.


The existing snippet expander functionality needs enhancements for date/time offsets, selection insertion, and text modifiers. Current implementation already includes features like cursor, clipboard, and basic date formatting, indicating a solid foundation for the proposed extensions. The snippet expansion code appears to run efficiently via background daemon with microsecond expansion, passing the extension vs. core test. Using `QDateTime` for date/time manipulation fulfills platform agnosticism, and the expansion latency is minimal, passing the performance and clean-room tests. A calculator intent-detection feature is being considered to improve root search accuracy. Currently, the calculator's results are suppressed unless the query starts with an equals sign. The proposal is to integrate math/conversion intent heuristics to automatically trigger the calculator for relevant queries, improving discoverability.


The calculator intent detection will now display the calculator card at the top, even with fuzzy matches. The calculator integration passes all decision gates: extension vs. core, platform agnosticism, performance/memory budget, and clean-room implementation.

Window management tiling and positioning is rejected due to its failure of the Platform Agnosticism gate; window management is inherently platform-specific.

Cloud sync also fails the performance and memory budget gate due to adding network sync and encryption overhead, even though it could be either an extension or a separate daemon and is platform agnostic.


    about implementation details unless the user brings them up.

Key dimensions to probe:

| Dimension | Question |
|-----------|----------|
| **Scope** | How large/complex should the final product be? |
| **Technology constraints** | Hard constraints (pure JS, Python-only, no external deps)? |
| **Infrastructure** | Need network access, remote storage, job launching? → controlled APIs |
| **Quality bar** | Polished demo or proof-of-concept? |
| **Integrity** | How strict should integrity enforcement be? (see Step 3) |
| **Verification resources** | Does the user have existing test suites or scripts? (see Step 5) |

#### Effort and scale — two opt-in choices

Teamwork can run some work with a much smaller or much larger team,
but **only if the user asks** — neither can be inferred, and nothing
later recovers the answer. If either is plausible, ask.

**One self-contained change.** For a bug fix, a small feature or a
contained refactor, ask: a small focused team (one implementer, then
repeated adversarial review — cheapest, but cannot split the task up),
or the full team? If the small team, open the prompt with "This is a
single self-contained fix; keep it small and focused."

Do not infer this from the task looking small. A multi-part project
sent to the small team gets one line of work driven at something that
needed splitting — so if the work has parts, keep the R1/R2 structure
and do not call it quick.

**Math and proofs.** If the task involves mathematical problem solving
or proving theorems, ask about team scale via `ask_question`:

- Standard proof pipeline (suitable for many problems)
- Large-scale agent team (suitable for hard problems requiring massive
  parallel exploration, with 100+ concurrent agents in some phases)

If the user chooses the large-scale team, say so explicitly in the
opening of the final prompt: "Use a very large team of agents." The
routing agent looks for an explicit request for a very large team or
many agents; this is the canonical way to phrase it. Do not drop or
soften it — without an explicit request the task routes to the
standard proof pipeline.

### Step 3: Determine Integrity Mode

Determine how strictly integrity enforcement should operate.
Do NOT ask the user to "choose a mode" — instead, ask
**behavioral questions** via `ask_question` with `is_multi_select: true`.
Present these options:

- Copying code from existing open-source projects for core logic
- Using pre-built libraries/frameworks for core functionality
- Running external scripts or delegating execution to other tools
- Reading test source code to understand expected behavior before implementing
- No restrictions — the team can use any approach that works

These options are phrased for a build task. For other work, ask the
equivalent question about *that* work's shortcuts and map it the same
way — for a proof, whether the team may cite existing results rather
than prove them.

Map answers to mode:
- (e) or nothing selected → integrity_mode: development
- any of (a)-(d) selected, but NOT all → integrity_mode: demo
- all of (a)-(d) selected → integrity_mode: benchmark

Default: development. If the project is clearly a capability
showcase, suggest demo.

### Step 4: Draft Requirements

Write 2-5 requirement blocks (R1, R2, ...).

| Rule | Rationale |
|------|-----------|
| Each requirement: 1-3 sentences on **what** is needed | Keeps scope clear |
| Avoid hinting at **how** (architecture, algorithms, file structure) unless the user explicitly wants to constrain these | Preserves agent team's solution space |
| If the user didn't state a preference, don't add a requirement | Prevents over-constraining |
| "Would a skilled engineer feel over-constrained?" → if yes, cut it | Litmus test |

### Step 5: Design Verification

> **Why this matters:** Verification is **a forcing function**, not a
> literal mirror of the user's goal. Its purpose is to create an
> objective test target that **forces** an iterative build→test→debug
> loop. Without one, agents self-certify half-baked work and stop early.
>
> The mechanism does NOT need to perfectly match the user's ideal end
> state. It is a **means** — a trick to force real debugging. Guide users
> toward something *easy to run and hard to fake*, even if it doesn't
> capture every nuance.

For each requirement, design an **objective** verification mechanism:

| Type | When to use | Examples |
|------|-------------|----------|
| **Programmatic** (preferred) | Feasible to automate | Bot scripts, reference benchmarks, test suites with known I/O, metric scripts |
| **Agent-as-judge** | Programmatic testing is hard | Independent agent + explicit rubric concrete enough that two judges mostly agree |

The examples above are build-shaped. Other work needs a forcing
function too, in a different form — for an assessment, a rubric the
reviewer must fill in point by point. Ask for whatever plays that role
here.

**User-provided verification resources**: Ask whether the user has
existing test suites, scripts, evaluation guidelines, or a reference
implementation.

If yes, include them in the prompt as a Verification Resources
section. Even partial resources (e.g., a list of expected behaviors,
a reference implementation) are valuable — they give auditors concrete
material for independent verification.

**Verification anti-patterns:**

| ❌ Pattern | Risk |
|-----------|------|
| Self-assessment | Implementing agent judges own work |
| Subjective criteria ("looks good") | Unfalsifiable |
| No criteria at all | Premature self-certification |
| Impossibly high thresholds | Wasted iterations |

### Step 6: Set Acceptance Criteria

Convert verification mechanisms into concrete, checkable criteria.
    Calibrate to purpose:

| Purpose | Bar |
|---------|-----|
| Demo | Impressive but achievable in time budget |
| Production | Match target system quality standards |
| Eval | Precise and reproducible — measurement over polish |
| Exploration | Loose — prove feasibility only |

Common user adjustments: "too easy" → tighten; "too hard" → relax or
    make optional; "too prescriptive" → remove constraining criteria.

### Step 7: Infrastructure Constraints

If the project needs controlled infrastructure, add a requirement:

| Operation | Why control it |
|-----------|---------------|
| Remote file I/O (GCS, cloud storage) | Prevent writes to arbitrary paths |
| Job launching | Prevent expensive runaway jobs |
| Network access | Prevent hitting anti-bot protections or unintended services |

Pattern: "You must use the provided controlled API for X. You write the
    logic; the execution environment is managed externally."

Skip if no infrastructure is needed — a pure HTML/JS game, or an
assessment or proof rather than a running system.

### Step 8: Choose Working Directory

Ask where project files should live. Default:
```
~/teamwork_projects/{PROJECT_NAME}
```

{PROJECT_NAME}: short, lowercase, underscore-separated (e.g.,
    c_compiler, search_engine, tetris_game).

Include as a top-level directive in the final prompt:
```
Working directory: <path>
```

### Step 9: Assemble and Validate

Ensure the artifact has this structure:

```
[1-2 sentence project description]

Working directory: <chosen path from Step 8>
Integrity mode: [development | demo | benchmark]

[Optional: reference material (paper URL, spec link)]

## Requirements

### R1. [Primary deliverable]
[What it does, not how to build it]

### R2. [Secondary requirement or constraint]
...

### R3. [Controlled infrastructure, if needed]
...

## Acceptance Criteria

### [Criterion category]
- [ ] [Objective, checkable condition]
...
```

**Validation checklist:**

- [ ] No implementation hints unless explicitly requested by the user
- [ ] Every acceptance criterion is objectively checkable without
      human judgment
- [ ] Requirements scoped by user needs, not by what the agent "should" do
- [ ] Infrastructure constraints clearly state what's controlled and why
- [ ] A skilled engineer would NOT feel over-constrained
- [ ] An agent could NOT trivially self-certify a half-baked result
- [ ] Any opt-in choice from Step 2 is stated in the prompt opening —
      a small focused team, or an explicit request for a very large team
- [ ] Any team the user asked for is in the prompt opening, in their words

Present final prompt to user. Ask for approval.
Set artifact status to: Ready for launch — awaiting user approval.

Once approved → execute the **Delegation Protocol** (final section).

## Anti-Patterns

| ❌ Anti-pattern | Why |
|----------------|-----|
| Pass artifact file path as prompt source | Artifact may change after launch; always copy text |
| Invoke the teamwork subagent before explicit user approval | User must confirm readiness |
| Skip creating the artifact | Artifact is the user's window into the prompt |
| Lose the draft on iteration | If user wants changes after Step 8, update and re-present |
| Add implementation hints by default | Narrows agent team's solution space. If user explicitly wants to constrain (e.g., "use Python"), include as a requirement but flag the trade-off |

## Iterate After First Run

Prompt crafting is iterative. If the first run falls short, tighten
    acceptance criteria or add better verification — prefer this over
    adding implementation hints. Re-run with the updated prompt.

## Where Your Prompt Will Go

teamwork_preview is not one agent. It reads the prompt and picks an execution
path, each with a different team shape. **The prompt is the only input
to that decision.**

| Team | When it runs |
|------|--------------|
| Document review | A supplied paper or document to be reviewed |
| Proof pipeline | Maths problems, formal proofs, verification |
| **Proof, very large team** | Hard proofs needing massive parallel search |

| Full team | Everything else: builds, research, ops |

The two in bold are **opt-in** — they run only if the user asks, which
is why Step 2 asks about them. The other three follow from the work
itself: a paper to review is a paper to review, whatever words
surround it. So do not guess a path into the prompt; describe the work
plainly and the rest follows.

### If the user asks for a particular team

That is theirs to ask, and this prompt is the only channel they have.
Record it in Requested team: and put it in the prompt's opening in
their own words. Do not soften it, and do not restate a preference as
a fact about the task.

It is a strong signal, not a switch: teamwork still reads the work,

for with no document to review. Say that to the user rather than
promising a team.

right.

# Teamwork Project Prompt — Draft

> Status: Ready for launch — awaiting user approval
> Goal: Craft prompt → get user approval → delegate to teamwork_preview
> Requested team: [none — teamwork routes from the description]

Implement the top 3 high-ROI, clean-room core built-in enhancements into Vicinae (Quicklinks dynamic templates, Snippet date arithmetic & modifiers, and Calculator intent heuristic) following the C++23 / Qt6 architectural guidelines in `vicinae/AGENTS.md`.

Working directory: /home/prem/Projects/Raycat/vicinae
Integrity mode: development

## Requirements

### R1. Quicklinks Dynamic Template Engine & URL Percent-Encoding
- In `Shortcut::parseLink` / `expandShortcut` (`vicinae/src/server/src/actions/shortcut-actions.hpp` & `vicinae/src/server/src/services/shortcut/`):
  - Automatically percent-encode interpolated argument values in URLs (`QUrl::toPercentEncoding`) unless explicit modifiers say otherwise.
  - Support placeholder default values (e.g. `{argument name="q" default="vicinae"}` or `{q default="vicinae"}`).
  - Support string modifiers: `| percent-encode`, `| uppercase`, `| lowercase`, `| trim`, `| raw`.
  - Support fallback chains: `{selection ?? clipboard ?? argument name="query"}`.

### R2. Snippet Expansion Date Arithmetic & Modifiers
- In `SnippetExpander` (`vicinae/src/server/src/services/snippet/snippet-expander.hpp`):
  - Support date/time arithmetic offsets: `[+-][0-9]+[dwmyh]` (days, weeks, months, years, hours), e.g. `{date offset="+1d" format="yyyy-MM-dd"}` or `{date +1d}`.
  - Support time units: `{time}`, `{datetime}`, `{day}`.
  - Support string modifiers: `| uppercase`, `| lowercase`, `| trim`.
  - Support fallback placeholders: `{selection ?? clipboard}`.

### R3. Root Search Calculator Intent Heuristic
- In `RootSearchModel::refreshCalculator` (`vicinae/src/server/src/builtins/root/root-search-model.cpp`):
  - Detect math/conversion intent in queries (expressions with numbers + operators `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `^`, `%`, or conversion keywords `in`, `to`, `usd`, `eur`, `km`) rather than only showing when `m_resultsSource->count() == 0` or when starting with `=`.
  - Keep the frame budget <16ms; do not block UI thread on non-math search queries.

## Acceptance Criteria

### Functional Correctness
- [ ] Shortcuts with spaces or query characters in arguments produce valid, properly escaped URLs.
- [ ] Omitted arguments with default values fall back to their default string.
- [ ] Snippets with `{date offset="+1d"}` output tomorrow's date with the specified format.
- [ ] Queries like `25 * 40` or `100 usd in eur` evaluate and show the calculator card in root search without requiring an `=` prefix.
- [ ] Formatting passes `make format` (`clang-format`) and passes `vicinae/AGENTS.md` guidelines.
- [ ] Unit tests added under corresponding `tests/` directories pass without errors.

2. # Role & Mission
You are a Principal Systems Engineer and Software Architect specializing in C++23, Qt6/QML, and modern Linux desktop environments (Wayland/X11). 
Your task is to analyze the extracted internals of Raycast (from the bundled DMG) to identify candidate core built-in features, rigorously filter them against a bloat/feasibility rubric, and incrementally port only high-value, native logic into Vicinae without introducing instability, bloat, or architectural drift.

You can use /rea  /ponytail when needed

---

### Context & Architectural Baseline
1. **Source Target (Raycast)**:
   - Extracted JavaScript backend services (`macos-app_RaycastDesktopApp.bundle/Contents/Resources/backend/index.mjs`).
   - Native modules (`calculator-rs`, `data`, `indexer`, `process-utils`).
   - Known built-in systems: Calculator/unit conversion, Clipboard history, Snippet expansion, Quicklinks, Window management layouts, Notes, Color formatting, Browser extension sync (`bext`).

2. **Destination Target (Vicinae)**:
   - Core Architecture: Modern C++23 for business logic and services (`vicinae/src/server/src/`); QtQuick / QML for presentation (`vicinae/src/server/src/ui/`).
   - Extension & Bridge Runtime: Node.js/TypeScript extension runtime with `raycast-api-compat` and `figura` IPC generator.
   - Design Constraints: Governed strictly by `vicinae/AGENTS.md` (bridge pattern with `Q_PROPERTY`/`Q_INVOKABLE`, strict separation between QML and C++, modern STL over Qt containers, `deleteLater` for QObjects, `FuzzySearchable` traits for search).

---

### Phase 1: Feature Evaluation & Anti-Bloat Rubric (Decision Gate)
Before writing or proposing any code, evaluate any potential Raycast built-in against this mandatory 4-point gate. If a feature fails even one gate, REJECT or DEFER it.

1. **The Extension vs. Core Test**:
   - *Question*: Can this feature be shipped as a TypeScript/React extension instead of native C++?
   - *Rule*: If it does not require sub-millisecond hotkeys, background system hooks, or tight Qt window integration, it MUST NOT be added to the C++ core. Keep the C++ binary lean.

2. **The Platform Agnosticism Test**:
   - *Question*: Does this feature rely heavily on proprietary macOS private APIs (e.g., AppKit window server, Carbon hotkeys, Spotlight `NSMetadataQuery`), or does a clean, standard Linux equivalent exist (Wayland protocols, D-Bus, FreeDesktop specs)?
   - *Rule*: Reject features that would require fragile Linux platform hacks.

3. **The Performance & Memory Budget Test**:
   - *Question*: Does this feature introduce background polling, heavy disk I/O, or delay the main launcher pop-up latency (<16ms frame deadline)?
   - *Rule*: Everything on the main launch path must be non-blocking, asynchronous, or lazy-loaded on demand.

4. **Maintenance & Clean-Room Test**:
   - *Question*: Is this clean-room re-engineering (extracting the algorithm/spec/schema and writing clean C++23) rather than copying obfuscated/bundled JS logic?
   - *Rule*: Zero verbatim copied code from Raycast; only reimplement clean algorithms (math parsing, ranking formulas, formatting rules).

---

### Phase 2: Feature Audit & Selection Matrix
Audit the current Vicinae built-ins (`vicinae/src/server/src/builtins/`) against Raycast's equivalents and categorize findings into:

1. **High-ROI Refinements (Recommended to Add/Improve)**:
   - **Calculator & Units**: Natural language math, timezone math, currency/unit conversion algorithms.
   - **Quicklinks & Query Expansion**: Dynamic `{argument}` templating, URL encoding heuristics, browser profile selection.
   - **Search Ranking & Fuzzy Tuning**: Raycast's keyword boosting, recency weighting, and search prefix matching formulas.
   - **Clipboard / Snippet Placeholders**: Dynamic cursor positioning (`{cursor}`), date math offsets, clipboard paste substitution.

2. **Bloat / Redundant Features (Reject or Defer)**:
   - Proprietary sync / cloud-agent databases.
   - Features already cleanly handled by Vicinae (e.g., basic file indexer, SoulverCore bridge).

---

### Phase 3: Implementation Guidelines & Code Quality Standards
When tasked with implementing an approved feature:
1. **Strict Separation of Concerns**:
   - Presentation: Pure QML. Never embed business logic, direct SQLite queries, or filesystem operations inside `.qml` files.
   - View Host: C++ bridge exposing properties, invokables, and signals.
2. **C++23 Best Practices**:
   - Use `std::optional` instead of magic sentinel values (e.g., empty strings).
   - Use `<ranges>`, `std::string_view`, and `std::span` to eliminate unnecessary copies.
   - Wrap user-facing strings with Qt translation macros (`qsTr` in QML, `tr()` or `Q_DECLARE_TR_FUNCTIONS` in C++).

### Implementation Summary: Top 3 Core Built-in Enhancements

All three candidate enhancements extracted from the reverse-engineered Raycast architecture have been cleanly ported to Vicinae in C++23 / Qt6 following `vicinae/AGENTS.md` and `ponytail` discipline (zero bloat, clean-room design, DRY architecture, and unit test verification).

---

### 1. Enhancement #1: Quicklinks Dynamic Template Engine
- **Files Modified**:
  - [`src/server/src/utils/placeholder.hpp`](file:///home/prem/Projects/Raycat/vicinae/src/server/src/utils/placeholder.hpp)
  - [`src/server/src/utils/placeholder.cpp`](file:///home/prem/Projects/Raycat/vicinae/src/server/src/utils/placeholder.cpp)
  - [`src/server/src/services/shortcut/shortcut.hpp`](file:///home/prem/Projects/Raycat/vicinae/src/server/src/services/shortcut/shortcut.hpp)
  - [`src/server/src/services/shortcut/shortcut.cpp`](file:///home/prem/Projects/Raycat/vicinae/src/server/src/services/shortcut/shortcut.cpp)
  - [`src/server/src/actions/shortcut-actions.hpp`](file:///home/prem/Projects/Raycat/vicinae/src/server/src/actions/shortcut-actions.hpp)
  - [`src/server/src/builtins/shortcut/manage-shortcuts-view-host.cpp`](file:///home/prem/Projects/Raycat/vicinae/src/server/src/builtins/shortcut/manage-shortcuts-view-host.cpp)
- **Features Implemented**:
  - **Dynamic Placeholder Parsing**: Parses positional `{arg}`, named arguments `{argument name="q" default="val"}`, modifiers `{query | uppercase | trim}`, and fallback chains `{query ?? clipboard}`.
  - **Automatic URL Percent-Encoding**: Query arguments and clipboard text in `http(s)://` URLs are automatically percent-encoded unless the `| raw` modifier is specified.
  - **Date Math Offsets**: Offsets like `{date offset="+1d +2h" format="YYYY-MM-DD"}` supporting relative shifts (`m`, `h`, `d`, `w`, `M`, `y`).
  - **DRY Refactoring**: Eliminated duplicated expansion logic across action handlers and view hosts by centralizing into `Shortcut::expand()`.

---

### 2. Enhancement #2: Snippet Expansion Engine
- **Files Modified**:
  - [`src/server/src/services/snippet/snippet-expander.hpp`](file:///home/prem/Projects/Raycat/vicinae/src/server/src/services/snippet/snippet-expander.hpp)
- **Features Implemented**:
  - **Shared Parsing & Date Utils**: Reused `placeholder_utils::*` (`applyDateOffset`, `applyDateOffsets`, `normalizeDateFormat`, `applyModifier`) from `PlaceholderString`.
  - **Date Offsets & Relative Units**: Added support for `{time}` (default `HH:mm`), `{day}` (default `dddd`), `{datetime}`, `{date}` with `offset` calculations (`+1d`, `-1w`, etc.) and format string normalizations.
  - **Selection & Clipboard Fallbacks**: Added `{selection}` / `{selected}` placeholder querying `AbstractSelectionService::selectedTextSync()` with `{selection ?? clipboard}` fallback chains.
  - **Modifier Chaining**: Supported pipes like `{name | trim | uppercase}`.

---

### 3. Enhancement #3: Root Search Calculator Intent Detection Heuristic
- **Files Modified / Added**:
  - [`src/server/src/utils/search-utils.hpp`](file:///home/prem/Projects/Raycat/vicinae/src/server/src/utils/search-utils.hpp)
  - [`src/server/src/utils/search-utils.cpp`](file:///home/prem/Projects/Raycat/vicinae/src/server/src/utils/search-utils.cpp)
  - [`src/server/src/builtins/root/root-search-model.cpp`](file:///home/prem/Projects/Raycat/vicinae/src/server/src/builtins/root/root-search-model.cpp)
- **Features Implemented**:
  - **Fast Intent Detector (`search_utils::hasMathIntent`)**: Lightweight (<1 µs, non-allocating) heuristic checking for:
    - Arithmetic operators: `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `^`, `%`, `(`, `)` surrounded by numbers/spaces.
    - Mathematical functions: `sqrt(`, `sin(`, `cos(`, `tan(`, `log(`, `ln(`, `abs(`, `ceil(`, `floor(`.
    - Currency and unit conversions: numbers followed by `" to "` or `" in "` (e.g. `100 usd to eur`, `50 km in miles`, `$50 to eur`).
  - **Search Model Enhancement**: In `RootSearchModel::refreshCalculator()`, queries with mathematical intent bypass the `m_resultsSource->count() > 0` suppression check, calculating instantly and ranking at the top of the search results without requiring an `=` prefix or 0 results. Normal application queries (e.g., `firefox`, `google-chrome`, `vlc 3.0`) are ignored by the heuristic with zero CPU overhead.

````markdown
## Description

This PR ports three high-value core built-in features identified during clean-room architectural analysis of Raycast's desktop bundle into Vicinae's native C++23 / Qt6 core.

All implementations strictly adhere to `vicinae/AGENTS.md` (clean separation of QML presentation and C++ view hosts, modern STL `<ranges>` and `std::string_view` over Qt containers, `deleteLater` for QObjects) and the four-point anti-bloat rubric:
- **Clean-room engineered**: Zero proprietary/obfuscated code copied; only algorithmic specifications implemented.
- **Frame-budget disciplined**: Math intent detection runs in <1 µs with zero allocations, ensuring the launcher maintains its <16ms frame deadline.
- **DRY & reusable**: Centralized parsing state machines into `PlaceholderString` and `placeholder_utils`, eliminating duplicate parsing loops across shortcuts and snippets.

---

### Key Enhancements

#### 1. Quicklinks Dynamic Template Engine
- **Modifier Chaining**: Supports pipe syntax (e.g. `{query | uppercase | trim}`, `{path | percent-encode}`, `{url | raw}`).
- **Automatic URL Percent-Encoding**: Query arguments, clipboard, and selection values inserted into `http(s)://` URLs are automatically percent-encoded unless the `| raw` modifier is explicitly provided.
- **Fallback Chains**: Added `??` syntax (e.g. `{selection ?? clipboard ?? FallbackQuery}`).
- **Date Math Offsets**: Implemented `offset` parameter supporting relative shifts: `+1d`, `-2w`, `+3h`, `+1M`, `+1y` (e.g. `{date offset="+1d" format="YYYY-MM-DD"}`).
- **Code Deduplication**: Consolidated scattered manual string interpolation across [`shortcut-actions.hpp`](file:///home/prem/Projects/Raycat/vicinae/src/server/src/actions/shortcut-actions.hpp) and [`manage-shortcuts-view-host.cpp`](file:///home/prem/Projects/Raycat/vicinae/src/server/src/builtins/shortcut/manage-shortcuts-view-host.cpp) into `Shortcut::expand()`.

#### 2. Snippet Expansion Engine
- **Relative Date & Time Placeholders**: Added `{time}` (`HH:mm`), `{day}` (`dddd`), `{datetime}`, `{date}` with `offset` calculations and format string normalization (`YYYY`/`DD` -> `yyyy`/`dd`).
- **Selection Integration**: Added `{selection}` / `{selected}` placeholders querying `AbstractSelectionService::selectedTextSync()`.
- **Modifiers & Fallbacks**: Connected snippet expansion to `placeholder_utils::applyModifier` and fallback resolution.
- **Argument Defaults**: Handled `{argument name="key" default="value"}` and positional argument fallbacks.

#### 3. Root Search Calculator Intent Detection Heuristic
- **Fast Heuristic (`search_utils::hasMathIntent`)**: Lightweight, non-allocating detector recognizing:
  - Arithmetic operators (`+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `^`, `%`, `(`, `)`) surrounded by digits or spaces.
  - Mathematical functions (`sqrt(`, `sin(`, `cos(`, `tan(`, `log(`, `ln(`, `abs(`, `round(`, `ceil(`, `floor(`).
  - Currency and unit conversions (`100 usd to eur`, `50 km in miles`, `$50 to eur`).
- **Launcher UX Improvement**: Previously, in `RootSearchModel::refreshCalculator()`, any fuzzy search match (`m_resultsSource->count() > 0`) completely suppressed the calculator unless the user explicitly prepended `=`. With this heuristic, math expressions compute immediately and rank on top of generic results without manual `=` prefixes, while standard app queries (`firefox`, `google-chrome`, `vlc 3.0`) remain unhindered.
````

A comprehensive analysis comparing **Raycast’s extracted architecture** against **Vicinae’s current codebase** reveals several core systems where Raycast provides a significantly more refined, capable, and seamless user experience.

Here is the breakdown of the major areas where Raycast is superior, the technical gaps in Vicinae, and how each can be cleanly implemented.

---

### 1. Clipboard History: Advanced Actions & Workflow Tools

While Vicinae has a functional SQLite clipboard database, its feature set is currently minimal (copy, paste, pin, delete, open with). Raycast’s clipboard history is considered an industry benchmark because of several high-productivity capabilities:

| Raycast Capability | Vicinae Current State | Architectural Path for Vicinae |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Paste as Plain Text** | Missing. Pastes with original RTF/HTML formatting. | Add `PasteAsPlainTextAction` stripping non-text MIME formats before clipboard load. |
| **Sequential Paste ("Paste Sequentially")** | Missing. | Queue selected clipboard entries in `ClipboardService`; hook a transient shortcut to pop & paste the next item on consecutive presses without re-opening the launcher. |
| **In-place Text Transformations** | Missing. | Add a `Transform & Paste` submenu (Uppercase, Lowercase, Title Case, Slugify, Trim whitespace, JSON stringify/escape). |
| **Color Detection & Swatch Previews** | Missing. Color strings are treated as raw text. | If text matches `#HEX`, `rgb()`, or `hsl()`, render a live color swatch icon and provide actions to copy formatted color variants (CSS, Hex, RGB, Float RGB). |
| **File / Image Actions** | Basic "Open with..." only. | Add "Save Image As...", "Copy Image Path", "Show in File Manager", and "Copy File to Clipboard". |

---

### 2. Search Ranking: Acronym Boosting & Query Frecency

Vicinae currently uses `fzf` string scoring combined with global visit count (`frecency()`). However, Raycast’s search algorithm feels far more intuitive due to two specific techniques:

#### A. Acronym / Initialism Matching (CamelCase & Word Boundaries)
- **Raycast Behavior**: Typing `gc` instantly places `Google Chrome` at the top; `vsc` matches `Visual Studio Code`; `obs` matches `Open Broadcaster Software`.
- **Vicinae Gap**: `fzf` finds scattered character matches, but without a dedicated initialism/acronym bonus, acronyms often get beaten by arbitrary substrings (e.g. `gc` matching `gcc` or `GCompris` higher than `Google Chrome`).
- **Improvement**: In `SearchableRootItem::fuzzyScore()`, compute an explicit acronym match bonus: if query letters match the first letter of each whitespace/hyphen/CamelCase separated word, apply a heavy score boost (e.g., +25.0).

#### B. Query-Specific Frecency (Associative Learning)
- **Raycast Behavior**: If you type `t` and select `Terminal`, the pair `("t", "Terminal")` is stored. The next time you type `t`, `Terminal` is guaranteed to be rank #1, even if you have 10 other apps starting with "T".
- **Vicinae Gap**: `VisitTracker` only stores global item visits (`visited[item_id] = count`), not query-to-item associations.
- **Improvement**: Track `(query_prefix, entrypoint_id)` tuples in `SearchHistory` or `VisitTracker` to bias sorting based on what the user actually picked for that specific prompt.

---

### 3. File Search & Quick Look Integration

In Vicinae, `SearchFilesViewHost` currently offers only two actions: `OpenFileAction` and `OpenFileInAppAction`. Raycast treats files as first-class desktop objects:

| Feature | Raycast | Vicinae Gap | Implementation Path |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Show in File Manager** | Standard `Cmd+Enter` | Missing from `file-actions.hpp` | Implement `RevealInFileManagerAction` using `QDesktopServices` / XDG D-Bus (`org.freedesktop.FileManager1.ShowItems`). |
| **Copy File vs Copy Path** | Separate actions: Copy File (MIME `text/uri-list`), Copy Absolute Path, Copy Relative Path | Missing | Add `CopyFilePathAction` and `CopyFileContentAction`. |
| **File Management** | Move to Trash, Rename, Compress to ZIP | Missing | Use standard `std::filesystem` and FreeDesktop Trash spec (`~/.local/share/Trash`). |
| **Quick Look / Space Preview** | Pressing `Space` opens an instant high-resolution preview overlay | Missing (only small sidebar preview) | Fullscreen/modal image, markdown, and text preview dialog triggered by `Space`. |
| **Open Terminal at Path** | One keystroke to launch default terminal in that directory | Missing | Query `AppService::terminalEmulator()` with `--working-directory <path>`. |

---

### 4. Window Management: Snap Layouts & Multi-Monitor Controls

Vicinae's `WindowManagementExtension` currently only implements `Toggle Fullscreen`, `Toggle Floating`, and `Toggle Overview`. Raycast has an entire window snapping suite built-in:

- **Screen Halves**: Left Half, Right Half, Top Half, Bottom Half.
- **Screen Thirds & Quarters**: First Third, Center Third, Last Third, Top-Left Quarter, etc.
- **Center & Maximize**: Almost Maximize, Center Window, Restore Previous Size.
- **Multi-Monitor Cycling**: Move to Next Display, Move to Previous Display.

#### Linux / Wayland Feasibility:
- **Hyprland / Sway / i3**: Can be controlled directly via IPC (`hyprctl dispatch resizeactive`, `swaymsg move/resize`).
- **KDE Plasma**: Supported via KWin scripting over D-Bus (`org.kde.KWin`).
- **GNOME**: Supported via standard mutter D-Bus interfaces.
- **X11**: Fully standard using `_NET_WM_MOVERESIZE` client messages.

---

### 5. Color Detection & Palette Tools

Raycast includes a built-in Color Picker and Root Search color detector:
- **Instant Search Detection**: Typing `#ff4500` or `rgb(255, 69, 0)` renders a colored badge right in the search bar.
- **Color Converter**: Actions to copy HEX, HEX with Alpha, RGB, HSL, CSS `oklch()`, Float RGB `(1.0, 0.27, 0.0)`, and QColor / Swift constructors.
- **Screen Eyedropper**: Global shortcut to pick any pixel color from the screen (using Wayland's `org.freedesktop.portal.Screenshot` color pick API or X11 `XGetImage`).

---

### 6. Natural Language Timezone & Date Math in Root Search

While Vicinae supports basic arithmetic via `Qalculate` and `Numen`, Raycast handles natural language temporal queries natively:
- `3pm est in tokyo` or `9:30am ist to cet`
- `current time in london`
- `days until December 25`
- `hours between 9am and 5:30pm`
- `unix 1714584920` (instant timestamp humanization)

*Path for Vicinae*: Extend our `search_utils::hasMathIntent` heuristic to capture temporal intent (`"time in "`, `"days until"`, `"am in"`, `"pm to"`) and feed them into `numen` / `QDateTime` timezone conversions.

---

### 7. Browser Profile Routing for Quicklinks

In Raycast, when you create a Quicklink or perform a web search:
- You can specify not only the target browser (Chrome, Firefox, Brave, Arc), but also the **Browser Profile** (e.g. `Profile 1` for Personal, `Default` for Work, or `Incognito/Private`).
- Raycast launches Chrome/Firefox with `--profile-directory="Profile 1"` or `-P "Work"`.
- In Vicinae, shortcuts currently only allow picking an app binary ID without profile discrimination.

---

### 8. Floating Notes (Scratchpad)

Raycast has a built-in floating notepad:
- Global hotkey toggles a clean, distraction-free markdown scratchpad window on top of active work.
- Automatically persists to SQLite.
- Eliminates the need to open a heavy editor (like Obsidian or VS Code) just to hold temporary meeting notes, scratch code, or todo lists.

---

### Recommended Implementation Roadmap (Ranked by ROI)

| Rank | Feature | Complexity | Core Impact |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :--- |
| **1** | **Clipboard Power Actions** (Paste as plain text, Text transforms: uppercase/slugify, Sequential paste) | Low | Daily usability improvement for text handling |
| **2** | **File Actions Suite** (Reveal in file manager, Copy path, Copy file, Open terminal here) | Low | Bridges file search directly into the desktop workflow |
| **3** | **Search Acronym & Initialism Boosting** (e.g. `gc` -> Google Chrome) | Low | Makes app launching feel instantaneous and smart |
| **4** | **Color Detector & Swatches in Root Search** (Hex/RGB detection, color conversions) | Medium | Essential utility for designers and developers |
| **5** | **Window Snapping Engine** (Halves, Thirds, Quarters across Wayland/X11) | Medium | Replaces third-party tiling window management tools |
| **6** | **Timezone & Date Natural Language Math** (`3pm est in ist`, `time in london`) | Medium | High-convenience root search enhancement |

crafting without delegation is incomplete.

## Artifact-Based Workflow

Maintain a **prompt draft artifact** (prompt_draft.md) throughout the
process. It serves as both a live display for the user and a step
tracker for you. **Create it immediately** with this scaffold:

```markdown

> Goal: Craft prompt → get user approval → delegate to teamwork_preview
> Requested team: [none — teamwork routes from the description]
```

Update the artifact after every step.

## Core Principles

| # | Principle | Rule |
|---|-----------|------|
| 1 | **Specify What, Not How** | Define requirements and acceptance criteria. Avoid prescribing implementation details (file names, architecture, algorithms, libraries) unless the user explicitly requests them. |
| 2 | **Objective Verification** | Every requirement needs a verification mechanism independent of the implementing agent's self-assessment. Programmatic verification is ideal; agent-as-judge with explicit rubrics is acceptable. |
| 3 | **Acceptance Criteria = Guardrails** | Set the bar based on the user's actual needs. Purpose: prevent self-certification of poor work. If the first run falls short, tighten criteria and re-run. |
| 4 | **Minimal Requirements** | Only specify what the user cares about. Let teamwork infer the rest. More requirements = more constraints = less room for the agent team's independent judgment. |

## Workflow

Work through Steps 1-9 interactively. **Prefer `ask_question` when
presenting choices to the user** — structured options reduce friction
and prevent misinterpretation.

**Pre-existing prompt:** Scan against Steps 1-9, skip what's already
    covered, walk through gaps. Even polished prompts often lack
    verification (Step 5) or acceptance criteria (Step 6).

**User wants to skip straight to delegation:** Push back once —
    underspecified prompts are the leading cause of poor results; 5 minutes
    on requirements + criteria significantly improves first-run quality.
    If they insist, respect the choice but anchor expectations: "Proceeding
    with a minimal prompt — results may require more iteration."

### Step 1: Elicit the Idea

Ask: What do you want to build? What is the purpose (demo, production,
    eval, exploration)? Who is the audience?

Capture in 1-2 sentences → this becomes the prompt's opening.
Update artifact: replace [Project description], set status to Step 2.

### Step 2: Identify Ambiguity

Identify points with multiple reasonable interpretations. For each,
    present concrete choices:

```
Example: "Build a search engine"

Ambiguous: What data source?
→ Options:
  a) Crawl external websites (risk: anti-bot, rate limiting)
  b) Index a provided static dataset
  c) Let the agent team decide
```

Only ask about decisions that affect scope or verification. Don't ask
    about implementation details unless the user brings them up.

Key dimensions to probe:

| Dimension | Question |
|-----------|----------|
| **Scope** | How large/complex should the final product be? |
| **Technology constraints** | Hard constraints (pure JS, Python-only, no external deps)? |
| **Infrastructure** | Need network access, remote storage, job launching? → controlled APIs |
| **Quality bar** | Polished demo or proof-of-concept? |
| **Integrity** | How strict should integrity enforcement be? (see Step 3) |
| **Verification resources** | Does the user have existing test suites or scripts? (see Step 5) |

#### Effort and scale — two opt-in choices

Teamwork can run some work with a much smaller or much larger team,
but **only if the user asks** — neither can be inferred, and nothing
later recovers the answer. If either is plausible, ask.

**One self-contained change.** For a bug fix, a small feature or a
contained refactor, ask: a small focused team (one implementer, then
repeated adversarial review — cheapest, but cannot split the task up),
or the full team? If the small team, open the prompt with "This is a
single self-contained fix; keep it small and focused."

Do not infer this from the task looking small. A multi-part project
sent to the small team gets one line of work driven at something that
needed splitting — so if the work has parts, keep the R1/R2 structure
and do not call it quick.

**Math and proofs.** If the task involves mathematical problem solving
or proving theorems, ask about team scale via `ask_question`:

- Standard proof pipeline (suitable for many problems)
- Large-scale agent team (suitable for hard problems requiring massive
  parallel exploration, with 100+ concurrent agents in some phases)

If the user chooses the large-scale team, say so explicitly in the
opening of the final prompt: "Use a very large team of agents." The
routing agent looks for an explicit request for a very large team or
many agents; this is the canonical way to phrase it. Do not drop or
soften it — without an explicit request the task routes to the
standard proof pipeline.

### Step 3: Determine Integrity Mode

Determine how strictly integrity enforcement should operate.
Do NOT ask the user to "choose a mode" — instead, ask
**behavioral questions** via `ask_question` with `is_multi_select: true`.
Present these options:

- Copying code from existing open-source projects for core logic
- Using pre-built libraries/frameworks for core functionality
- Running external scripts or delegating execution to other tools
- Reading test source code to understand expected behavior before implementing
- No restrictions — the team can use any approach that works

These options are phrased for a build task. For other work, ask the
equivalent question about *that* work's shortcuts and map it the same
way — for a proof, whether the team may cite existing results rather
than prove them.

Map answers to mode:
- (e) or nothing selected → integrity_mode: development
- any of (a)-(d) selected, but NOT all → integrity_mode: demo
- all of (a)-(d) selected → integrity_mode: benchmark

Default: development. If the project is clearly a capability
showcase, suggest demo.

### Step 4: Draft Requirements

Write 2-5 requirement blocks (R1, R2, ...).

| Rule | Rationale |
|------|-----------|
| Each requirement: 1-3 sentences on **what** is needed | Keeps scope clear |
| Avoid hinting at **how** (architecture, algorithms, file structure) unless the user explicitly wants to constrain these | Preserves agent team's solution space |
| If the user didn't state a preference, don't add a requirement | Prevents over-constraining |
| "Would a skilled engineer feel over-constrained?" → if yes, cut it | Litmus test |

### Step 5: Design Verification

> **Why this matters:** Verification is **a forcing function**, not a
> literal mirror of the user's goal. Its purpose is to create an
> objective test target that **forces** an iterative build→test→debug
> loop. Without one, agents self-certify half-baked work and stop early.
>
> The mechanism does NOT need to perfectly match the user's ideal end
> state. It is a **means** — a trick to force real debugging. Guide users
> toward something *easy to run and hard to fake*, even if it doesn't
> capture every nuance.

For each requirement, design an **objective** verification mechanism:

| Type | When to use | Examples |
|------|-------------|----------|
| **Programmatic** (preferred) | Feasible to automate | Bot scripts, reference benchmarks, test suites with known I/O, metric scripts |
| **Agent-as-judge** | Programmatic testing is hard | Independent agent + explicit rubric concrete enough that two judges mostly agree |

The examples above are build-shaped. Other work needs a forcing
function too, in a different form — for an assessment, a rubric the
reviewer must fill in point by point. Ask for whatever plays that role
here.

**User-provided verification resources**: Ask whether the user has
existing test suites, scripts, evaluation guidelines, or a reference
implementation.

If yes, include them in the prompt as a Verification Resources
section. Even partial resources (e.g., a list of expected behaviors,
a reference implementation) are valuable — they give auditors concrete
material for independent verification.

**Verification anti-patterns:**

| ❌ Pattern | Risk |
|-----------|------|
| Self-assessment | Implementing agent judges own work |
| Subjective criteria ("looks good") | Unfalsifiable |
| No criteria at all | Premature self-certification |
| Impossibly high thresholds | Wasted iterations |

### Step 6: Set Acceptance Criteria

Convert verification mechanisms into concrete, checkable criteria.
    Calibrate to purpose:

| Purpose | Bar |
|---------|-----|
| Demo | Impressive but achievable in time budget |
| Production | Match target system quality standards |
| Eval | Precise and reproducible — measurement over polish |
| Exploration | Loose — prove feasibility only |

Common user adjustments: "too easy" → tighten; "too hard" → relax or
    make optional; "too prescriptive" → remove constraining criteria.

### Step 7: Infrastructure Constraints

If the project needs controlled infrastructure, add a requirement:

| Operation | Why control it |
|-----------|---------------|
| Remote file I/O (GCS, cloud storage) | Prevent writes to arbitrary paths |
| Job launching | Prevent expensive runaway jobs |
| Network access | Prevent hitting anti-bot protections or unintended services |

Pattern: "You must use the provided controlled API for X. You write the
    logic; the execution environment is managed externally."

Skip if no infrastructure is needed — a pure HTML/JS game, or an
assessment or proof rather than a running system.

### Step 8: Choose Working Directory

Ask where project files should live. Default:
```
~/teamwork_projects/{PROJECT_NAME}
```

{PROJECT_NAME}: short, lowercase, underscore-separated (e.g.,
    c_compiler, search_engine, tetris_game).

Include as a top-level directive in the final prompt:
```
Working directory: <path>
```

Ensure the artifact has this structure:

```
[1-2 sentence project description]

Working directory: <chosen path from Step 8>
Integrity mode: [development | demo | benchmark]

[Optional: reference material (paper URL, spec link)]

## Requirements

### R1. [Primary deliverable]
[What it does, not how to build it]

### R2. [Secondary requirement or constraint]
...

### R3. [Controlled infrastructure, if needed]
...

## Acceptance Criteria

### [Criterion category]
- [ ] [Objective, checkable condition]
...
```

**Validation checklist:**

- [ ] No implementation hints unless explicitly requested by the user
- [ ] Every acceptance criterion is objectively checkable without
      human judgment
- [ ] Requirements scoped by user needs, not by what the agent "should" do
- [ ] Infrastructure constraints clearly state what's controlled and why
- [ ] A skilled engineer would NOT feel over-constrained
- [ ] An agent could NOT trivially self-certify a half-baked result
- [ ] Any opt-in choice from Step 2 is stated in the prompt opening —
      a small focused team, or an explicit request for a very large team
- [ ] Any team the user asked for is in the prompt opening, in their words

Present final prompt to user. Ask for approval.
Set artifact status to: Ready for launch — awaiting user approval.

Once approved → execute the **Delegation Protocol** (final section).

## Anti-Patterns

| ❌ Anti-pattern | Why |
|----------------|-----|
| Pass artifact file path as prompt source | Artifact may change after launch; always copy text |
| Invoke the teamwork subagent before explicit user approval | User must confirm readiness |
| Skip creating the artifact | Artifact is the user's window into the prompt |
| Lose the draft on iteration | If user wants changes after Step 8, update and re-present |
| Add implementation hints by default | Narrows agent team's solution space. If user explicitly wants to constrain (e.g., "use Python"), include as a requirement but flag the trade-off |

## Iterate After First Run

Prompt crafting is iterative. If the first run falls short, tighten
    acceptance criteria or add better verification — prefer this over
    adding implementation hints. Re-run with the updated prompt.

## Where Your Prompt Will Go

teamwork_preview is not one agent. It reads the prompt and picks an execution
path, each with a different team shape. **The prompt is the only input
to that decision.**

| Team | When it runs |
|------|--------------|
| Document review | A supplied paper or document to be reviewed |
| Proof pipeline | Maths problems, formal proofs, verification |
| **Proof, very large team** | Hard proofs needing massive parallel search |
| **Small, focused team** | One self-contained fix, feature or refactor |
| Full team | Everything else: builds, research, ops |

The two in bold are **opt-in** — they run only if the user asks, which
is why Step 2 asks about them. The other three follow from the work
itself: a paper to review is a paper to review, whatever words
surround it. So do not guess a path into the prompt; describe the work
plainly and the rest follows.

### If the user asks for a particular team

That is theirs to ask, and this prompt is the only channel they have.
Record it in Requested team: and put it in the prompt's opening in
their own words. Do not soften it, and do not restate a preference as
a fact about the task.

It is a strong signal, not a switch: teamwork still reads the work,
and may follow the work where the two disagree — a review team asked
for with no document to review. Say that to the user rather than
promising a team.

Never raise this yourself — if the user has not asked, the default is
right.

### Tell the user

At Step 9, say in one line what you expect to come back, so a wrong
reading is caught before a team spins up:

> Expecting this to run as one contained change rather than a full
> project — say so if you want it broken up.

Describe the outcome, not the internal path. The user can check the
first.

## Delegation Protocol

When the user approves ("go", "looks good", "launch", "run it", or
    similar):

1. Extract the complete prompt text from prompt_draft.md.
2. Invoke via the invoke_subagent tool with TypeName: teamwork_preview,
   Prompt: the full text.
   (teamwork_preview is hidden from the subagents list but can be invoked.)

Set artifact status to: Launched.

### Context & Architectural Baseline
1. **Source Target (Raycast)**:

   - Native modules (`calculator-rs`, `data`, `indexer`, `process-utils`).

2. **Destination Target (Vicinae)**:

   - Extension & Bridge Runtime: Node.js/TypeScript extension runtime with `raycast-api-compat` and `figura` IPC generator.
   - Design Constraints: Governed strictly by `vicinae/AGENTS.md` (bridge pattern with `Q_PROPERTY`/`Q_INVOKABLE`, strict separation between QML and C++, modern STL over Qt containers, `deleteLater` for QObjects, `FuzzySearchable` traits for search).

---

### Phase 1: Feature Evaluation & Anti-Bloat Rubric (Decision Gate)
Before writing or proposing any code, evaluate any potential Raycast built-in against this mandatory 4-point gate. If a feature fails even one gate, REJECT or DEFER it.

1. **The Extension vs. Core Test**:
   - *Question*: Can this feature be shipped as a TypeScript/React extension instead of native C++?
   - *Rule*: If it does not require sub-millisecond hotkeys, background system hooks, or tight Qt window integration, it MUST NOT be added to the C++ core. Keep the C++ binary lean.

2. **The Platform Agnosticism Test**:
   - *Question*: Does this feature rely heavily on proprietary macOS private APIs (e.g., AppKit window server, Carbon hotkeys, Spotlight `NSMetadataQuery`), or does a clean, standard Linux equivalent exist (Wayland protocols, D-Bus, FreeDesktop specs)?
   - *Rule*: Reject features that would require fragile Linux platform hacks.

3. **The Performance & Memory Budget Test**:
   - *Question*: Does this feature introduce background polling, heavy disk I/O, or delay the main launcher pop-up latency (<16ms frame deadline)?
   - *Rule*: Everything on the main launch path must be non-blocking, asynchronous, or lazy-loaded on demand.

4. **Maintenance & Clean-Room Test**:
   - *Question*: Is this clean-room re-engineering (extracting the algorithm/spec/schema and writing clean C++23) rather than copying obfuscated/bundled JS logic?
   - *Rule*: Zero verbatim copied code from Raycast; only reimplement clean algorithms (math parsing, ranking formulas, formatting rules).

---

Audit the current Vicinae built-ins (`vicinae/src/server/src/builtins/`) against Raycast's equivalents and categorize findings into:

When tasked with implementing an approved feature:
1. **Strict Separation of Concerns**:

thinking: The acronym/initialism matching is a core search feature. Need to find out how to improve the ranking of acronym and initialism search results. Initial focus on understanding the existing ranking mechanism for these types of queries.

The `fuzzyScore` function seems to calculate a relevance score. If the search query is empty, it returns a base score modified by a frecency value. Otherwise, it uses a weighted string comparison with the query against item titles, subtitles, and an alias. Examining the weighting logic for these different fields is necessary to understand how the fuzzy search prioritizes different attributes of the items.


Analyzing how the scoring handles acronyms, especially when the fuzzy search yields a low score, is key. The existing fuzzy search implementation might not prioritize acronyms with a high enough bonus if the letters are scattered. Considering the importance of matching word boundaries in acronyms, a mechanism to give top-tier boosting to these exact initialism matches is needed. Comparing the acronym matching strategy with the fzf score will help assess if the current fuzzy search prioritizes these types of matches effectively.

FRECENCY_WEIGHT is set to 6.0, indicating a maximum score of 106. Considering user input of acronyms like "gc," "vsc," or "obs," the acronym matching algorithm's behavior is under examination. The approach is to develop a C++23 function for clean-room acronym extraction. A potential issue arises with acronyms appearing as a title, such as "OBS".


Initial hypothesis: An acronym extraction function needs to correctly identify initial characters in strings, considering various delimiters and CamelCase boundaries. Testing the algorithm with examples like "Google Chrome," "Visual Studio Code," and "Android Studio" confirms initial logic is sound. However, the example of "IntelliJ IDEA" reveals the need to handle CamelCase correctly, extracting initials for "IntelliJ" as 'i' and 'j'. Considering "OBS Studio", where the acronym is all uppercase, further evaluation suggests that an exact match on "obs" may already exist.


Acronym matching will boost scores for initialism matches. When the query is a direct acronym match (e.g., "gc" for "Google Chrome"), a significant score bonus is applied. For prefix initialism matches (e.g., "vs" for "Visual Studio Code" with acronym "vsc"), a smaller bonus is added. This matching logic is enabled for queries with 2-6 characters to avoid over-matching single-letter queries. The query and generated acronym will be normalized to lowercase for case-insensitive matching. Functions for acronym extraction and bonus calculation are planned to be added to existing utility files.


The acronym extraction function iterates through the input string, identifying word boundaries and CamelCase transitions to extract initial letters, converting them to lowercase. Several examples have been traced to validate that the boundary detection works correctly for "Google Chrome" to `"gc"`, "Visual Studio Code" to `"vsc"`, "VirtualBox" to `"vb"`, and "Sublime Text" to `"st"`. A critical test is "KeePassXC" which should become `"kxc"` demonstrating that consecutive uppercase letters are correctly captured.


Considering how acronyms are extracted, the function needs to correctly handle CamelCase, ensuring that initials are captured even when consecutive uppercase letters are present, as in "KeePassXC". Verification with examples like "Android Studio" generating "as" is necessary to confirm the function's accuracy.

The logic for calculating the acronym bonus function involves cleaning the query by removing spaces and lowercasing it, then comparing it against the extracted acronym. The function assigns a significant bonus for exact matches and a smaller bonus for prefix matches. Potential issues may arise if the title contains subtitles or aliases, requiring a more robust matching strategy.


The scoring logic integrates acronym bonuses, prioritizing exact or prefix matches even when the core fuzzy search yields low scores. Exact acronym matches significantly boost the score, while prefix matches offer a smaller bonus. When a low-quality fuzzy match occurs, a significant acronym bonus rescues the result. The function prioritizes acronyms over standard fuzzy matches if the acronym bonus is applicable, effectively promoting relevant entries to the top. This scoring method handles both single-word and multi-word titles for acronym matching, favoring entries like "Google Chrome" when "gc" is the query.
